researchUpdates.title: Formation of Zeolite Phases in Alkali-Activated Binders and Their Role in the Immobilization of Toxic Elements
researchUpdates.summary: A critical review connects zeolite-phase formation in alkali-activated binders with mechanisms that can retain potentially toxic elements, organizing evidence around precursor chemistry, activation and curing conditions.
highlights: Zeolite crystallization is treated as a conditional outcome within an alkali-activated matrix, so precursor composition and processing history must accompany any immobilization claim.

Retention within a reaction product is not automatically equivalent to long-term leach resistance; element identity, speciation, exposure medium, test duration and leaching protocol remain necessary evidence.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher-indexed metadata and searchable article excerpts only because direct MDPI article access returned HTTP 429 during review. The record is a synthesis of prior studies, not a new independent immobilization experiment. Individual precursor systems, zeolite assignments, toxic elements and leaching conditions were not fully audited, so no universal retention efficiency or service-life claim is made.
researchUpdates.summaryBasis: Primary MDPI publisher metadata and indexed article excerpts; no abstract text, publisher highlights, figures, tables or full-paper passages were reproduced

journalArticle.title: A phase name is not a leach test
journalArticle.summary: Zeolite formation can help explain toxic-element retention, but mineral identification alone does not establish durable immobilization.
paragraphs: Alkali-activated binders can contain amorphous gels alongside crystalline or semicrystalline zeolite phases. Which phases form depends on the precursor, activator, available silica and alumina, curing temperature and time, so the phase label cannot be separated from the preparation route.

For the evidence database, pair every immobilization result with the element and oxidation state, phase-identification method, mixture chemistry, curing history and leaching protocol. A structural explanation is valuable, but it should not replace measured release under the exposure conditions relevant to the intended wasteform.
